content.title: WHY YOUR {{HEALTHY}} MEAL PREP IS QUIETLY BACKFIRING
facts: **Overcrowding the pan** – Piling vegetables into one crowded pan traps steam, so they boil in their own moisture instead of browning, leaving you with soggy, flavorless food that's harder to enjoy in a balanced diet.

**Skipping the fat** – Many 'diet' recipes drain all oil to cut calories, but doing this blocks absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K hiding in those same vegetables. Add 1 tsp olive oil back in.
**Boiling leafy greens** – Dunking spinach or kale into a big pot of water leaches minerals straight into the liquid you then pour down the drain. Steam for 3-4 minutes instead.
**Same seasoning every time** – Relying only on salt for flavor trains your taste buds to expect it everywhere, making truly fresh, unsalted food taste bland by comparison.
**Pre-salting meat too early** – Salting chicken or fish right before cooking draws out moisture and dries it out; salt at least 20 minutes ahead, or right at the end.
**Cooking protein straight from the fridge** – Tossing cold meat into a hot pan causes uneven cooking, so the outside overcooks while the inside stays underdone. Let it sit out 15-20 minutes first.

**Not resting meat after cooking** – Cutting into chicken or steak immediately pushes out all the juices onto the cutting board; resting 5-10 minutes keeps meals moist and satisfying, so you're less tempted to overeat.
**One giant pot of rice or pasta for the week** – Reheating the same starch daily without variety spikes boredom fast, which is often what quietly derails 'healthy eating' plans by day four.

content.caption:
Let's talk about a few of these in more detail. Overcrowding the pan isn't just about looks — when vegetables steam instead of sear, they actually lose some of their natural sugars into the extra liquid, which is part of why they taste flat and watery instead of caramelized and sweet. Skipping the fat is a sneaky one too: vitamins A, E and K are fat-soluble, meaning your body literally cannot absorb them properly without some oil or fat present in the same meal, no matter how many greens you eat. And boiling leafy greens like spinach sends water-soluble nutrients like vitamin C and folate straight into the cooking water, so unless you're drinking that water, a lot of the benefit disappears down the sink. Everyone's kitchen habits are different, so start with the one that sounds most like you.
